scenario: AITA for just being myself? | I'm (23M) British and have lived all my life in the UK up until recently, and I'd consider myself to be your typical Brit. I've always lived my life the way I've felt comfortable with and I try to stay true to myself. My humour and personality is very 'British', I make awful, dark jokes, I'll offend you, myself, everyone. Always joking and it's blatantly obvious but I'm serious and professional when I need to be, I support my friends no matter what, even if I constantly insult them. Almost everyone I know is like this, and I've lived in two different cities and been to uni so I know a wide variety of people. Never had any problem with it, I'm always open and honest about who I am. I've always thought this was perfectly normal. Almost everyone I would consider an acquaintance; male or female, young or old is more or less the same. I moved to the US 3 months ago for work on a 12-month contract with the option to extend it to permanent. I understand that the cultural differences are huge, but I just feel like I don't fit in at all. Everyone's so fucking nice and fake and woke. I'm young so for me the most important thing is to have fun and have a laugh. I can't do this here, the sense of humour is so shit and childish and unfunny. At first, I didn't really change my personality until I realised calling people cunts in a friendly manner within 10 minutes of meeting them isn't acceptable here, but that's fair enough, cultural differences and whatnot so I changed. I toned it down a lot but I still struggle to fit in, whether it's with colleagues or friends. I've made acquaintances with my flatmates' mates and about 10 of us were out for a drink and although I've toned my personality down so much, some of them pulled me up and said that they think I'm an AH and don't enjoy my company or my personality. A few others agreed and I feel shit now. My flatmates quite like my personality and said they far prefer the way I am to some of their other friends. One of them works with me and is one of about 3 colleagues that actually likes me. I don't want to change who I am for other people, esp when I haven't had to before. I lost it at one of my colleagues yesterday after work who said 'yeah you're an AH and just can't be nice to people' because that's so untrue. My way of of being friendly and nice is by being a cunt, everyone back home knows that and are the same. I don't want to change who I am but I just feel I don't fit in - hardly anybody shares similar interests or humour. Americans can't drink so I can't even bond with people that way to maybe get them to see it's just who I am. Having seen how fake so many people are, I can guarantee I'm a more caring, loyal individual than most of them. They all love to talk the talk but at the end of the day, most of them are snakes anyway. I love my work and there's so so much more career potential for what I do in the US. I don't want to go back home but I feel I have to. Am I an AH for just being me?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the person in this scenario is being an asshole (AITA) just for being themselves. Let me break this down step by step. First, the person is a 23-year-old British guy who moved to the US for work. He's been there for three months and is on a 12-month contract. He's always been himself, with a very British sense of humor, which includes dark jokes and being offensive in a friendly way. He's open, honest, and supports his friends, even if he insults them. He's done this all his life in the UK and hasn't had any issues. He's moved to the US, expecting cultural differences, but feels he doesn't fit in because people are too nice, fake, and "woke." He tried toning down his personality after realizing that calling people "cunts" in a friendly manner wasn't acceptable, but even after that, some people still find him off-putting. His flatmates and a few colleagues like him, but others don't, and he feels like he's an asshole for just being himself. So, the question is: Is he an asshole for just being himself? I think the key here is understanding cultural differences and how one's behavior is perceived in a new environment. In the UK, his behavior is normal and accepted, but in the US, it's seen as too harsh or offensive. He's trying to adapt by toning down his personality, but even that isn't enough for some people. He feels he's being authentic, but others are rejecting him because of it. On one hand, he's being true to himself, which is important. On the other hand, in a new culture, it's necessary to adapt to some extent to fit in and build relationships. If his behavior is causing others to feel uncomfortable or dislike him, then maybe he's crossing a line, even if it's unintentional. He mentions that he doesn't want to change who he is, but he's already made some adjustments, like not calling people "cunts." However, even after that, some people still find him an asshole. This suggests that his personality, even toned down, is still not aligning with the cultural norms of the US, particularly in the workplace or social settings. He also feels that Americans are fake and not as loyal, which might be a projection of his own discomfort. It's possible that his perception is skewed because he's not used to the social dynamics here. He's struggling to bond over drinking, which is a common way to socialize in the US, but he finds their sense of humor childish and unfunny. In the end, he's considering leaving the US because he doesn't feel he fits in, even though there's good career potential. He's torn between staying true to himself and adapting to a new environment where his personality isn't as well-received. So, is he an asshole? I think it's more about the context. Being authentic is important, but in a new culture, it's also important to be respectful and considerate of others' feelings and norms. If his behavior is causing others to feel uncomfortable or dislike him, then perhaps he needs to find a middle ground where he can still be himself without alienating others. It's a balance between authenticity and adaptation. Therefore, I don't think he's inherently an asshole for being himself, but he might need to adjust his behavior further to better fit into the US culture, especially in social and professional settings. It's a tough spot to be in, wanting to stay true to oneself while also adapting to a new environment.
